unit_description: This is the culminating Grade 3 unit. Students solve length, weight, and liquid-volume problems, solve mixed measurement problems in the same units, write and solve two-step equations with unknowns, and estimate, solve, and evaluate reasonableness. The unit ends with a cumulative evaluation.
unit_goals: Solve length, weight, and liquid-volume problems.
Solve mixed measurement problems in the same units.
Write and solve two-step equations with unknowns.
Apply all four operations in real-world measurement contexts.

weeks.weekly_focus: Students apply the four operations to solve measurement problems, write two-step equations, and reason about answers.

lessons.lesson_title: Solve Length, Weight, and Liquid-Volume Problems
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by identifying whether a problem uses length, weight, or volume and which operation to use.
lessons.concept: Measurement word problems use the four operations. Use the same units within a problem. Add to combine, subtract to compare, multiply for equal groups, and divide to share.
lessons.practice: Solve one-step word problems involving length, weight, and liquid volume.
lessons.objective: Solve length, weight, and liquid-volume problems.

questions.prompt: A bottle holds 2 liters. If you pour out 500 milliliters, how much is left?
A rope is 18 feet long. You cut off 7 feet. How long is it now?
Four water bottles hold 1 liter each. How many liters total?

learn.title: Solve Length, Weight, and Liquid-Volume Problems
teaching_points: Read the problem to find the measurement type.

example.prompt: A box weighs 12 pounds. Another box weighs 8 pounds. What is the total weight?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A jug holds 3 liters. You pour it into 6 equal cups. How much is in each cup?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Solve each measurement word problem. Make sure units match.

bigIdea.title: Solve Length, Weight, and Liquid-Volume Problems
bigIdea.subtitle: Use the right unit and operation
bigIdea.intro: Measurement problems can be solved with addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division. The key is to use the same units and pick the operation that matches the situation.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: Why must units match before you add or subtract?

ruleCards.description: Only add or subtract measurements with the same unit.
Use the operation that fits the problem.

lessons.lesson_title: Solve Mixed Measurement Problems in the Same Units
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by converting between units within the same system before solving.
lessons.concept: Sometimes a problem gives measurements in different units. Convert to the same unit before adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing.
lessons.practice: Convert measurements and solve mixed measurement problems.
lessons.objective: Solve mixed measurement problems in the same units.

learn.title: Solve Mixed Measurement Problems in the Same Units
teaching_points: Convert to the same unit first.
Use known relationships: 1000 mL = 1 L, 1000 g = 1 kg, 12 in = 1 ft.

example.prompt: A jug has 1.5 liters of water. You add 500 milliliters. How many liters total?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A ribbon is 2 feet long. Another ribbon is 18 inches long. What is the total length in inches?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Convert to the same unit, then solve each problem.

bigIdea.title: Solve Mixed Measurement Problems in the Same Units
bigIdea.subtitle: Convert before you compute
bigIdea.intro: When measurements use different units, convert them to the same unit before solving. It is like making sure you are comparing apples to apples.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: Why is it important to convert before adding?

ruleCards.description: Change one unit to match the other.
Now you can add because the units match.

lessons.lesson_title: Write and Solve Two-Step Equations With Unknowns
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by writing equations for one-step word problems before moving to two steps.
lessons.concept: Two-step word problems may need two operations and an unknown. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown and solve it step by step.
lessons.practice: Write and solve two-step equations for word problems.
lessons.objective: Write and solve two-step equations with unknowns.

questions.prompt: Jill had 5 liters. She bought 2 more liters and poured 3 liters out. Write an equation for how much she has now, l.
A tank holds 10 gallons. 3 gallons leak out each hour. How many gallons are left after 2 hours?
A piece of wood is cut into 3 equal parts. Each part is 18 inches. What was the original length?

learn.title: Write and Solve Two-Step Equations With Unknowns
teaching_points: Use a letter for the unknown.
Write the operations in the order they happen.

example.prompt: A bucket had 4 liters. You add 2 liters, then pour out 3 liters. How much is left?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A box weighs 6 pounds. You put in two 4-pound bags. What is the total weight?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Write an equation with an unknown and solve each two-step problem.

bigIdea.title: Write and Solve Two-Step Equations With Unknowns
bigIdea.subtitle: Use a letter for the unknown
bigIdea.intro: Two-step problems often have an unknown. Use a letter like w or x for the unknown, write the operations that happen, and solve one step at a time.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How does writing an equation help solve a two-step problem?

ruleCards.description: A letter stands for the unknown amount.
Write the operations in the order they happen in the story.

lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by estimating an answer before computing.
lessons.concept: Estimation helps you check if an answer makes sense. Round numbers, solve, then compare the exact answer to the estimate to evaluate reasonableness.
lessons.practice: Estimate, solve, and check reasonableness for measurement and operation problems.

questions.prompt: A watermelon weighs 4 pounds. Is 8 ounces a reasonable weight?
questions.hint: 8 ounces is half a pound; a watermelon is much heavier.

learn.title: Estimate, Solve, and Evaluate Reasonableness
teaching_points: Compare the exact answer to the estimate.

example.prompt: A crate weighs 49 pounds. Another weighs 52 pounds. Estimate and find the total.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A road is 198 miles long. You drive 103 miles. Estimate and find how many miles are left.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Estimate, solve, and decide if each answer is reasonable.

bigIdea.title: Estimate, Solve, and Evaluate Reasonableness
bigIdea.subtitle: Check if your answer makes sense
bigIdea.intro: Estimation gives you a quick answer to compare against. If your exact answer is far from your estimate, you may have made a mistake. Reasonableness helps catch errors.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How does estimation help you evaluate reasonableness?

ruleCards.description: Use rounded numbers to find an approximate answer.
If exact and estimate are close, the answer is reasonable.

lessons.fact_drill: Rapid review of all Grade 3 topics for the cumulative evaluation.
lessons.concept: This cumulative evaluation reviews key topics from across Grade 3, with a focus on measurement and four-operation problem solving.
lessons.objective: Show what you have learned in Grade 3.

warmup.title: Luma Charge
warmup.instructions: Get ready to show what you know.

questions.prompt: A jar has 2 liters of juice. You pour 800 milliliters. How many milliliters are left?
A rope 42 inches long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
A book weighs 1 pound. Is 20 ounces a reasonable guess for its weight?
questions.hint: 1 pound = 16 ounces; 20 ounces is more than a pound.

learn.title: Ready to Show What You Know
teaching_points: Use any strategy that helps you.

example.prompt: This is the final Grade 3 evaluation.
example.equation: measurement + mixed units + two-step equations + reasonableness = Grade 3 readiness

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A fish tank holds 10 liters. You add 3 liters and then pour out 2 liters. How much is left?

practice_block.title: Cumulative Grade 3 Evaluation
practice_block.instructions: Answer all questions carefully to show your understanding of Grade 3.

flashcards.title: Unit 36 Review
flashcards.instructions: Review key terms from Unit 36 before the evaluation.

bigIdea.title: Cumulative Grade 3 Evaluation
bigIdea.subtitle: Show what you have learned
bigIdea.intro: This cumulative evaluation checks your understanding of the big ideas from this unit and across Grade 3. Take your time, read carefully, and show your thinking.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: What have you learned in Grade 3?

ruleCards.description: Make sure units match before adding or subtracting.
Use an estimate to see if the exact answer is reasonable.
